text.div:
SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD

  • Evaluation of chronic cough with blood-streaked sputum: three sputum samples at least eight hours apart, one early morning, for acid-fast smear, nucleic acid amplification and mycobacterial culture (including nontuberculous mycobacteria) and routine bacterial culture; interferon-gamma release assay and HIV test; blood count, CRP and metabolic panel; CT of the chest within a week; a mask in shared spaces until the smears are negative; call 911 or go to the emergency department for more than a few teaspoons of blood, blood with breathlessness, or chest pain
  • Urgent pulmonology consultation within one week for chronic productive cough with blood-streaked sputum: exclude tuberculosis, confirm or exclude bronchiectasis and plan its care, and advise on opioids and the lungs
  • Long-term opioid therapy review: prescription monitoring program checked (one prescriber, one pharmacy), urine drug test consistent with morphine only, naloxone prescribed and taught, no benzodiazepines or other sedatives, DSM-5-TR assessment (no opioid use disorder), dose continued unchanged with no forced taper, benefits and harms reviewed at every visit and at least every three months, the monitoring program checked with every prescription, and buprenorphine offered if opioid use disorder ever develops
  • Prolonged grief disorder therapy with the clinic psychologist, weekly for sixteen sessions, by video at first so she need not travel; PHQ-9 at every visit
  • Collaborative safety plan with warning signs, coping steps, people to contact, the clinic number and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; morphine kept in a locked box with only the current bottle out; safety reviewed at every visit
  • Bone and nutrition: vitamin D3 2000 units daily with a recheck at twelve weeks; DXA for low weight, vitamin D deficiency, limited weight-bearing and long-term opioid therapy; calcium-rich foods, small frequent meals and an oral supplement drink with the clinic dietitian; weight at every visit
  • Bronchiectasis care: active cycle of breathing with an oscillating positive expiratory pressure device twice daily, taught by the respiratory physiotherapist; a home exercise program; influenza, pneumococcal and COVID-19 vaccines; a written exacerbation plan with a sputum sample and amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 14 days; sputum culture at each review and spirometry, Bronchiectasis Severity Index and mycobacterial culture yearly; no long-term macrolide while exacerbations are fewer than three a year
  • Opioid dose reduction at her request: morphine lowered by about 10 percent at a time (to 18 mg a day now), with each step held at least four weeks, paused at any time she wishes, and never forced; withdrawal symptoms and sleep reviewed at each visit
  • Exacerbation of bronchiectasis: sputum culture before the first dose; amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 14 days; airway clearance three to four times a day; fluids; the morphine dose unchanged and no added cough suppressant; nurse phone check in two days; call 911 for more than a few teaspoons of blood, worsening breathlessness or confusion

resource.title: Elizabeth Barrett Browning synthetic care plan
resource.description: Evaluate chronic productive cough with blood-streaked sputum in a 39-year-old poet who has been an invalid for years and has taken a prescribed opioid since adolescence: test for tuberculosis first (three sputum samples for acid-fast smear, nucleic acid amplification and culture, an interferon-gamma release assay, and masking until the smears are negative), then confirm bronchiectasis by CT and work up its cause on the BTS 2019 guideline (blood count, immunoglobulins, Aspergillus serology, sputum bacterial and mycobacterial cultures including nontuberculous mycobacteria), with spirometry, airway clearance, vaccines, an exacerbation plan with a 14-day antibiotic, and clear rules for when hemoptysis needs emergency care; review long-term opioid therapy respectfully on the CDC 2022 guideline (benefits and harms, no forced taper, naloxone, the prescription monitoring program, urine drug testing, and DSM-5-TR criteria, under which tolerance and withdrawal from prescribed use do not count, so physiological dependence is not opioid use disorder; buprenorphine would be offered if it were present), and support the slow reduction she chooses; recognize and treat prolonged grief disorder with grief-focused psychotherapy, measurement-based follow-up and a safety assessment with safety planning; check bone health (vitamin D, DXA) and weight; and protect her writing. Her real illness remains undiagnosed; this record shows one modern possibility, not an answer.
